The government’s priorities for telecommunications include improving high-speed broadband coverage. Investment in telecommunications is primarily driven by the private sector in Canada, with targeted government funding and regulatory actions supporting broadband deployment in certain rural and remote regions where private sector investment is lacking. Several measures have been implemented or are underway. Innovation Agenda On June 14, 2016, the Government of Canada released its Innovation Agenda which puts forward a vision to build Canada as a global centre of innovation. The Innovation Agenda focuses on six areas of action: 1. Promoting an entrepreneurial and creative society 2. Supporting global science excellence 3. Building world-leading clusters and partnerships 4. Growing companies and accelerating clean growth 5. Competing in a digital world 6.Improving ease of doing business. A public consultation process for the Innovation Agenda is currently underway. One of the six pillars of the agenda is “competing in a digital world,” which will touch on issues related to broadband. The ongoing public consultation process is expected to help shape an innovation action plan. Federal government broadband program In Budget 2016, the federal government announced plans to invest up to $500 million over five years for a new program to extend and enhance broadband service in rural and remote communities. This new program will bring transformative, high-speed broadband infrastructure to communities in rural and remote parts of the country, with a focus on new backbone infrastructure (although backbone capacity upgrades and resiliency, as well as last-mile infrastructure projects are also eligible). Applications for funding are currently under review. The new program builds on the previous Connecting Canadians program (CCP) which provided funding over five years (2014 - 2019) to extend and enhance broadband Internet access to approximately 300,000 households across rural and remote communities in Canada. CCP also included a Northern funding component for the approximately 12,000 satellite-dependent households in northern communities in Nunavut and the Nunavik region of Northern.CRTC Modern telecommunications servicesIn December 2016, the CRTC issued Telecom Regulatory Policy 2016-496 establishing a new universal service objective that consists of: Canadians, in urban, rural and remote areas, having access to voice and broadband Internet access services, on both fixed and mobile wireless networks. In order to measure the successful achievement of this objective, the CRTC has determined that: 1. Canadian residential and business fixed broadband subscribers should be able to access speeds of at least 50 Mbps download / 10 Mbps upload, and subscribe to a service offering an unlimited data allowance; and 2. the latest generally deployed mobile wireless technology should be available not only in Canadian homes and businesses, but on as many major transportation roads as possible in Canada. The CRTC is also establishing a fund to support broadband projects in areas that do not meet these targets - the fund will provide up to $750 million over the first five years. A public proceeding is currently underway to establish the broadband funding regime (http://www.crtc.gc.ca/eng/archive/2017/2017-112.htm).

The government’s priorities for telecommunications include improving high-speed broadband coverage. Investment in telecommunications is primarily driven by the private sector in Canada, with targeted government funding and regulatory actions supporting broadband deployment in certain rural and remote regions where private sector investment is lacking. Since 2014, the Department for Innovation Science and Economic Development implemented two funding programs to expand broadband access in rural and remote areas:1)The Connecting Canadians program was launched in 2014 and allocated funding for projects to install the “last-mile” connection for 280,000 households that did not have access to broadband speeds of 5/1 Mbps. From 2015 to 2019, a total of CAD$290M in grants and contributions funds were allocated to Connecting Canadians, the program is ending in 2020.2)The Connect to Innovate program launched in 2016. It is a five-year, CAD$500-million program and it is focused on bringing high-speed Internet to 300 rural and remote communities in Canada. The program supports over 220 different projects across Canada with the potential to impact 390,000 households. The program provides support for backbone infrastructure to institutions such as schools and hospitals. It also includes funding for backbone upgrades and for last-mile connections to households and businesses that do not have access to broadband speeds of 5/1 Mbps. When completed, these projects will bring high-speed Internet access to approximately 975 rural and remote communities, including 190 Indigenous communities. Most are currently in the building phase, and many are expected to be completed in 2020.In Budget 2019, the Government of Canada made the commitment to connect all Canadians to reliable high-speed Internet at minimum speeds of 50/10 Mbps. The new Universal Broadband Fund will provide up to CAD$1 billion over 10 years to support broadband projects across Canada, it is being designed to meet the unique needs of rural and remote communities, and it is expected to launch in spring 2020.In December 2016, the CRTC issued Telecom Regulatory Policy 2016-496 establishing a new universal service objective that consists of: Canadians, in urban, rural and remote areas, having access to voice and broadband Internet access services, on both fixed and mobile wireless networks. The CRTC is also establishing a fund to support broadband projects in areas that do not meet these targets - the fund will provide up to CAD$750 million over the first five years. The government’s priorities for telecommunications include improving high-speed broadband coverage. Investment in telecommunications is primarily driven by the private sector in Canada, with targeted government funding and regulatory actions supporting broadband deployment in certain rural and remote regions where private sector investment is lacking. Since 2014, the Department for Innovation Science and Economic Development implemented two funding programs to expand broadband access in rural and remote areas:1)The Connecting Canadians program was launched in 2014 and allocated funding for projects to install the “last-mile” connection for 280,000 households that did not have access to broadband speeds of 5/1 Mbps. From 2015 to 2019, a total of CAD$290M in grants and contributions funds were allocated to Connecting Canadians, the program is ending in 2020.2)The Connect to Innovate program launched in 2016. It is a five-year, CAD$500-million program and it is focused on bringing high-speed Internet to 300 rural and remote communities in Canada. The program supports over 220 different projects across Canada with the potential to impact 390,000 households. The program provides support for backbone infrastructure to institutions such as schools and hospitals. It also includes funding for backbone upgrades and for last-mile connections to households and businesses that do not have access to broadband speeds of 5/1 Mbps. When completed, these projects will bring high-speed Internet access to approximately 975 rural and remote communities, including 190 Indigenous communities. Most are currently in the building phase, and many are expected to be completed in 2020.In Budget 2019, the Government of Canada made the commitment to connect all Canadians to reliable high-speed Internet at minimum speeds of 50/10 Mbps. The new Universal Broadband Fund will provide up to CAD$1 billion over 10 years to support broadband projects across Canada, it is being designed to meet the unique needs of rural and remote communities, and it is expected to launch in spring 2020.In December 2016, the CRTC issued Telecom Regulatory Policy 2016-496 establishing a new universal service objective that consists of: Canadians, in urban, rural and remote areas, having access to voice and broadband Internet access services, on both fixed and mobile wireless networks. In order to measure the successful achievement of this objective, the CRTC has determined that: 1)Canadian residential and business fixed broadband subscribers should be able to access speeds of at least 50/10 Mbps, and subscribe to a service offering an unlimited data allowance; and2)The latest generally deployed mobile wireless technology should be available not only in Canadian homes and businesses, but on as many major transportation roads as possible in Canada. The CRTC is also establishing a fund to support broadband projects in areas that do not meet these targets - the fund will provide up to CAD$750 million over the first five years. The selected projects from the first call for applications are expected to be announced by the CRTC in 2020. The deadline for submissions to the second call for applications for funding is 30 April 2020.

The government’s priorities for telecommunications include improving high-speed broadband coverage. Investment in telecommunications is primarily driven by the private sector in Canada, with targeted government funding and regulatory actions supporting broadband deployment in certain rural and remote regions where private sector investment is lacking. Since 2014, the Department for Innovation Science and Economic Development implemented two funding programs to expand broadband access in rural and remote areas:1)The Connecting Canadians program was launched in 2014 and allocated funding for projects to install the “last-mile” connection for 280,000 households that did not have access to broadband speeds of 5/1 Mbps. From 2015 to 2019, a total of CAD$290M in grants and contributions funds were allocated to Connecting Canadians, the program is ending in 2020.2)The Connect to Innovate program launched in 2016. It is a five-year, CAD$500-million program and it is focused on bringing high-speed Internet to 300 rural and remote communities in Canada. The program supports over 220 different projects across Canada with the potential to impact 390,000 households. The program provides support for backbone infrastructure to institutions such as schools and hospitals. It also includes funding for backbone upgrades and for last-mile connections to households and businesses that do not have access to broadband speeds of 5/1 Mbps. When completed, these projects will bring high-speed Internet access to approximately 975 rural and remote communities, including 190 Indigenous communities. Most are currently in the building phase, and many are expected to be completed in 2020.In Budget 2019, the Government of Canada made the commitment to connect all Canadians to reliable high-speed Internet at minimum speeds of 50/10 Mbps. The new Universal Broadband Fund will provide up to CAD$1 billion over 10 years to support broadband projects across Canada, it is being designed to meet the unique needs of rural and remote communities, and it is expected to launch in spring 2020.In December 2016, the CRTC issued Telecom Regulatory Policy 2016-496 establishing a new universal service objective that consists of: Canadians, in urban, rural and remote areas, having access to voice and broadband Internet access services, on both fixed and mobile wireless networks. In order to measure the successful achievement of this objective, the CRTC has determined that: 1)Canadian residential and business fixed broadband subscribers should be able to access speeds of at least 50/10 Mbps, and subscribe to a service offering an unlimited data allowance; and2)The latest generally deployed mobile wireless technology should be available not only in Canadian homes and businesses, but on as many major transportation roads as possible in Canada. The CRTC is also establishing a fund to support broadband projects in areas that do not meet these targets - the fund will provide up to CAD$750 million over the first five years. The selected projects from the first call for applications are expected to be announced by the CRTC in 2020. The deadline for submissions to the second call for applications for funding is 30 April 2020.

dataValue: India has signed international agreements managing cross border flows on data privacy.Cross-border data access requests are governed both by the local laws of the country making the request, and those of the jurisdiction where the entity receiving the request or its data storage facility is based. Often, these laws may limit personal data access by third parties, including foreign government agencies. The normal route to gain access to data under such circumstances is through the use of MLATs (mutual legal assistance treaties). As of November 2019, India had entered into MLATs with forty-two countries and was a signatory to six international conventions with mutual legal assistance provisions.
